name: Robin Hood of Sherwood: outlaw of the greenwood
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The foundational figure ladder that anchors all downstream Merry Men ladders (§16 teach-before-test). Robin Hood as he actually appears in the earliest surviving ballads, the fifteenth-century texts collected by Francis James Child as Child Ballads 117 (A Gest of Robyn Hode), 119 (Robin Hood and the Monk) and 118 (Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne). T1: ROBIN HOOD is an OUTLAW who lives in SHERWOOD FOREST in the county of NOTTINGHAM in the middle of England; he leads a band of outlaws called the MERRY MEN and wears LINCOLN GREEN so as to be hidden among the leaves. T2: he is a YEOMAN -- not a lord, not a peasant, but a free commoner -- and the earliest ballads say his 'gret courtesye' means he never robs a poor plowman or an honest woman traveller; his hatred is for CORRUPT ABBOTS, CHEATING SHERIFFS, and the arrogantly rich clergy. T3: the famous line 'ROBS FROM THE RICH AND GIVES TO THE POOR' is a LATER PARAPHRASE (the phrase in that form belongs to the eighteenth and nineteenth-century retellings, especially Joseph Ritson 1795 and Howard Pyle 1883). The Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117, c. 1450 in print but older in circulation) actually says Robin's charity is to distressed KNIGHTS and impoverished YEOMEN -- generosity within his class, not modern class-warfare. T4: his WEAPON is the ENGLISH LONGBOW -- the same weapon that had just, in the century before the ballads were printed, won Crecy (1346) and Agincourt (1415) for the English crown against France. His mastery of the longbow is the reason the ballads glow with archery-contests -- the longbowman was the folk hero of that generation. T5: the honest LEGENDARY-VS-HISTORICAL rail: NO historical Robin Hood has ever been proven; the name 'Robert Hod' and its variants shows up in thirteenth-century court records as a generic OUTLAW-NICKNAME the way 'John Doe' does today, and the ballads are LEGEND -- the fun is in the ballads, not in the impossible search for a real man. Further rungs: the ballads set the tale in the reign of an 'Edward' (Gest of Robyn Hode names Edward), NOT Richard the Lionheart -- the Richard-the-Lionheart-and-Bad-King-John setting is a Sir Walter Scott ADDITION in Ivanhoe (1819); the Merry Men in the earliest ballads number only Little John, Much the Miller's Son, and Will Scathelock (Scarlet) -- Friar Tuck and Maid Marian JOIN LATER; the outlaw wears a HOOD (the surname 'Hood' probably comes from that hood, not the other way round).
source: PRIMARY: A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child Ballad 117, printed c. 1500 by Wynkyn de Worde but circulating a century earlier); Robin Hood and the Monk (Child 119, MS c. 1450); Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne (Child 118, MS c. 1650 but attested earlier). SCHOLARLY: J. C. Holt, Robin Hood (1982; rev. 2011) -- 'Robert Hod' as generic thirteenth-century outlaw-nickname; Stephen Knight, Robin Hood: A Mythic Biography (2003). LATER PARAPHRASE: Joseph Ritson, Robin Hood: A Collection of All the Ancient Poems (1795); Howard Pyle, The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood (1883); Sir Walter Scott, Ivanhoe (1819) -- Richard-and-John setting is Scott's addition. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Robin Hood' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Robin Hood', 'A Gest of Robyn Hode', 'Child Ballads', 'Historicity of Robin Hood'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Child numbering and the earliest attested date for the 'robs from the rich' phrasing.
framing_note: The FOUNDATIONAL Robin Hood ladder -- this is the T1/T2 teach-before-test anchor that every other Merry Men ladder (Little John, Guy of Gisborne, Robin's death, etc.) will reference. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the 'robs from the rich and gives to the poor' line is NOT in the medieval ballads -- it is Ritson/Pyle nineteenth-century paraphrase) and T5 (there is no proven historical Robin Hood; 'Robert Hod' was a generic outlaw-nickname). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the outlaw of Sherwood' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a green-clad archer under an oak, a band of yeomen hidden in a leaf-thick forest, a longbow across his back) and let the recall be the OUTLAW, the FOREST, or the WEAPON. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Cuchulainn of Ulster or Roland at the pass -- a folk hero at the anchor of a body of song. DISTRACTOR MINE: other English medieval outlaws (Hereward the Wake, Adam Bell, William Wallace -- Wallace is Scottish and a real historical figure, adjacent), other forest-outlaws (William Tell in the Alps, Fulk FitzWarin -- an actual thirteenth-century outlaw whose story fed the Robin Hood legend), other legendary bowmen (Roland with Durandal is a swordsman, not archer; Odysseus with his bow; the Welsh archers of Crecy as a group). Wrong king-setting: NOT Richard the Lionheart in the ballads themselves -- that is Sir Walter Scott's Ivanhoe embellishment.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual thirteenth to fifteenth-century English longbowmen at Crecy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415) as military history; theology owns the FOLK HERO who represents them in song. HISTORY owns Fulk FitzWarin the real outlaw and any historical 'Robert Hod' in court rolls; theology owns the LEGEND that grew around them. GEOGRAPHY owns Sherwood Forest and the Major Oak as a real place; theology owns what HAPPENED in it in ballad.

name: Little John: John Little of the quarterstaff, renamed by inversion
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: Robin's second-in-command and the joke behind his name, from the seventeenth-century broadside Robin Hood and Little John (Child Ballad 125) and A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117). T1: LITTLE JOHN is Robin Hood's second-in-command in Sherwood and the strongest fighter in the Merry Men. T2: his REAL NAME is JOHN LITTLE -- and he is called 'Little John' as an IRONIC INVERSION, because he stands (in the ballads) SEVEN FEET TALL and is the BIGGEST man in the band. Renaming him 'Little John' is a joke the outlaws play the day he joins. T3: the story of his joining, in the broadside Robin Hood and Little John (Child 125): Robin meets a stranger crossing a NARROW BRIDGE over a stream. Neither will step aside for the other. They agree to fight with QUARTERSTAVES (long wooden staves, the poor man's weapon of the English commons) -- whoever is knocked off the bridge into the water loses. T4: JOHN LITTLE, the stranger, KNOCKS ROBIN OFF THE BRIDGE with his staff -- Robin falls into the water. Robin, laughing, wades out, blows his HORN to summon his men, and offers the winner a place in the band. When Will Stutely re-christens him 'Little John' by pouring water on him and inverting his name, the whole band celebrates. T5: in A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117) Little John is Robin's constant companion through every escapade -- carrying Robin's message to the poor knight Sir Richard at the Lee, disguising himself as a servant in the Sheriff's house, and (at the end) at Robin's deathbed at Kirklees Priory. Little John supposedly SURVIVES Robin and BURIES him. Further rungs: an ancient grave in HATHERSAGE churchyard in Derbyshire has for centuries been pointed out as Little John's -- an unusually long grave-mound; the quarterstaff was the standard weapon of English commoners because the longbow required years of training and swords were for gentry -- Little John's staff signals his social class; 'John' was the commonest English name of the period -- 'John Little' is almost a stand-in for 'ordinary Englishman'.
source: PRIMARY: Robin Hood and Little John (Child Ballad 125, broadside c. 17th century); A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117, Little John's role as constant companion, the Sir Richard at the Lee errand, Robin's death at Kirklees). SCHOLARLY: J. C. Holt, Robin Hood (1982) -- name-inversion joke; Stephen Knight, Robin Hood (2003). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Little John' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Little John', 'Robin Hood and Little John', 'Hathersage' -- John Little's real name, the quarterstaff bridge duel, seven-foot height, the Hathersage grave. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether 'Robin Hood and Little John' predates the Gest or postdates it in scholarly consensus.
framing_note: The SECOND-IN-COMMAND ladder -- introduces both Little John and the trope of the quarterstaff-on-the-bridge duel that becomes iconic in every later retelling. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (his real name is JOHN LITTLE, and he's called 'Little John' as a JOKE because he's the BIGGEST) and T4 (the newcomer KNOCKS ROBIN INTO THE WATER and gets rewarded with a place in the band). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Robin's giant second-in-command' AND ask who he is; describe the SCENE (a narrow log across a stream, two men with wooden staves, one splashed into the water) and let the recall be the NAME, the WEAPON, or the WINNER. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Patroclus beside Achilles or Oliver beside Roland -- a great warrior's inseparable second. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Merry Men (Friar Tuck, Will Scarlet, Alan-a-Dale, Much the Miller's Son -- all adjacent-real, all from the same ballads), other quarterstaff heroes, other 'ironic name' figures (King Little John of England -- adjacent-real historical figure, easily confused). Wrong weapon: QUARTERSTAFF, not longbow, not sword.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the real historical King John of England (1199-1216) whom Ivanhoe stitches into the legend; theology owns the outlaw LITTLE JOHN of the ballads. GEOGRAPHY owns Hathersage churchyard as a real Derbyshire village; theology owns the LEGEND of the giant grave there.

name: Friar Tuck: the fighting friar with a sword and a hound
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The stout warrior-priest of the Merry Men, from the broadside Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar (Child Ballad 123) and the fragment of the play Robin Hood and the Friar (c. 1475). T1: FRIAR TUCK is a FAT FRIAR (a wandering member of a mendicant order) who lives in Sherwood Forest and belongs to Robin Hood's band; he wears a friar's ROBE with a rope belt and carries a SWORD, being both a churchman and a fighting man. T2: he is NOT one of the original Merry Men of the earliest ballads -- Friar Tuck JOINS the Robin Hood tradition around the fifteenth century, first attested in a fragmentary play Robin Hood and the Friar around 1475 and in the broadside Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar (Child 123). T3: the story of his joining, in Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar: Robin, hearing of a stout friar living at Fountains Abbey who has beaten every man that came against him, goes to find him. Robin makes the friar CARRY HIM ACROSS THE RIVER on his back. Halfway across, the friar dumps Robin into the water in revenge for having been made to carry him. T4: they fight in the river with SWORDS all afternoon until they are both exhausted; the friar then WHISTLES up his fifty MASTIFFS (huge English hounds), and Robin whistles up his Merry Men -- neither side can beat the other, so Robin invites the friar to join the band. T5: the historical FRIAR TUCK behind the character may be a real fifteenth-century Sussex outlaw whom the royal writs of King Henry V (1417) named as 'Frere Tuk' -- a chaplain-turned-outlaw who terrorised the Sussex forests; the ballad-friar borrows the name and adds the merry-monk trimmings. Further rungs: 'CURTAL FRIAR' means a friar who wore a SHORT ROBE (from Old French 'curt' = short) -- a mendicant on the move; Tuck's fifty mastiffs are the real seed of Robin Hood's later dog-and-huntsman iconography; Tuck's sword and his willingness to fight are the joke -- CHURCHMEN WERE FORBIDDEN TO SHED BLOOD, so friars technically had to fight with clubs (see the 'club of the priest' rule in canon law) -- Tuck breaks the rule cheerfully; the classic image of a rotund tonsured friar with a leather flask of ale is Howard Pyle's nineteenth-century embellishment.
source: PRIMARY: Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar (Child Ballad 123, broadside c. 17th century); Robin Hood and the Friar (fragmentary play c. 1475). HISTORICAL: royal writ of Henry V 1417 naming a real Sussex outlaw 'Frere Tuk'. SCHOLARLY: J. C. Holt, Robin Hood (1982) -- Tuck as a fifteenth-century add-on to the earlier band; Stephen Knight, Robin Hood (2003). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Friar Tuck' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Friar Tuck', 'Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar', 'Sussex Frere Tuk of 1417'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact date of the play fragment and citation for the 1417 writ.
framing_note: The FIGHTING-FRIAR ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T3+T4 (Tuck CARRIES Robin across the river and DUMPS him in revenge; then Tuck whistles up FIFTY MASTIFFS to face the Merry Men). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the sword-swinging friar in Sherwood' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a stout tonsured monk with a sword-belt, a hound-pack at his heel, a river-crossing prank) and let the recall be the FRIAR, the WEAPON, or the HOUND. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Archbishop Turpin fighting beside Roland at Roncesvalles or Bishop Odo swinging his club at Hastings -- the WARRIOR-CLERIC trope, honoured across Christian pillars. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Merry Men (Little John, Will Scarlet, Alan-a-Dale, Much), other fighting churchmen (Archbishop Turpin from the Song of Roland, Bishop Odo of Bayeux -- both adjacent-real from history), other real-outlaw sources for legendary characters. Wrong order: TUCK is not in the earliest ballads -- he JOINS LATER, around 1475.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual medieval mendicant orders (Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites) and the 1417 real-outlaw Frere Tuk; theology owns the LEGEND-friar of the ballads.

name: Maid Marian: the May-Day queen who wandered into Sherwood
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: Robin's beloved, and the honest story of her ORIGIN outside the Robin Hood ballads. T1: MAID MARIAN is Robin Hood's sweetheart in the popular tradition -- a noblewoman who leaves her home to live with the outlaws in Sherwood Forest. T2: she is NOT in the earliest Robin Hood ballads. A Gest of Robyn Hode, Robin Hood and the Monk, and Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne (the three oldest Child ballads) have NO female love interest at all -- the only woman in the Gest is the villainous Prioress of Kirklees. T3: Marian comes from a SEPARATE FRENCH TRADITION -- the pastoral courtship songs of the shepherdess MARION and her shepherd-lover ROBIN, sung in the Jeu de Robin et Marion by Adam de la Halle (c. 1283). These songs travel across the Channel and become the centrepiece of the English MAY-DAY GAMES, where a village crowns a MAY QUEEN and calls her MARIAN and a village boy plays her lover ROBIN. T4: over the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries the May-games ROBIN and the ballad ROBIN HOOD are FUSED in village performance; the May Queen Marian becomes Robin's beloved. By the time Anthony Munday writes his plays The Downfall of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon (1598) and The Death of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon (1601), Maid Marian is a full-fledged member of the Merry Men, disguises herself as a boy to live in the forest, and matches her lover shot for shot with the bow. T5: the honest note is that Marian is a MAY-DAY IMPORT, not a medieval-outlaw original -- her tale of cross-dressing warrior-love is later ROMANCE grafted onto the older ballads. The romance succeeds because it FILLS A GAP the older tradition left: the outlaw hero needed a beloved, and the folk games had already given him one. Further rungs: 'Maid Marian' in some Elizabethan texts is a slang term for a woman of easy virtue or for a man dressed as a woman in Morris dances -- the reputation of the May-games heroine varies; in the modern Robin Hood tradition Marian is often given the surname 'Fitzwater' or made a ward of the crown -- these are Victorian inventions; she is often confused with the historical Maid of Norway or the Fair Rosamund -- both entirely separate figures.
source: PRIMARY: Adam de la Halle, Jeu de Robin et Marion (c. 1283, French pastoral play). Anthony Munday, The Downfall of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon (1598) and The Death of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon (1601) -- the Elizabethan plays that lock Marian into the Robin Hood story. NEGATIVE PRIMARY: A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117), Robin Hood and the Monk (Child 119), Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne (Child 118) -- all three lack Marian. SCHOLARLY: J. C. Holt, Robin Hood (1982) -- Marian's May-games origin; Stephen Knight, Robin Hood: A Mythic Biography (2003) -- the fusion process. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Maid Marian' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Maid Marian', 'Jeu de Robin et Marion', 'May Day tradition'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: date range for the fusion (c. 1500-1550) and the Munday plays.
framing_note: The MAID MARIAN honest-origin ladder -- the wonder is that she comes from OUTSIDE the ballads, from French May-Day pageants. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (Marian is NOT in the earliest Robin Hood ballads at all) and T3 (she came from a French shepherdess-and-shepherd love song by Adam de la Halle around 1283). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Robin Hood's beloved' AND ask her name; describe the SCENE (a May queen crowned in a village square, a French pastoral of a shepherdess and her shepherd, a woman shooting a bow beside Robin) and let the recall be the FIGURE, the FRENCH SOURCE, or the FESTIVAL. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Guinevere added to the Arthur legend by Chretien or the Norse Sigrdrifa woven into the Sigurd cycle -- a beloved GRAFTED onto an older hero-story. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Robin Hood women (the Prioress of Kirklees who kills him, adjacent-real from the ballads), other medieval heroine's-name confusions (Fair Rosamund the mistress of Henry II, the Maid of Norway who died en route to marry Edward II, Guinevere of Arthurian myth), other May-Day figures. Wrong text: NOT in the medieval ballads -- her fusion is Elizabethan.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns actual medieval Marys and Maids (the Maid of Norway, Fair Rosamund) and the actual May-Day village-games custom; theology owns the LEGEND-Marian and her fusion into Robin's story.

name: Will Scarlet, Much the Miller's Son, Alan-a-Dale: the other Merry Men
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The rest of the ballad-band, from A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117), Robin Hood and the Monk (Child 119), and Robin Hood and Allen a Dale (Child 138). T1: besides ROBIN, LITTLE JOHN and FRIAR TUCK, three other named MERRY MEN appear in the ballads -- MUCH THE MILLER'S SON, WILL SCARLET, and ALAN-A-DALE. T2: MUCH THE MILLER'S SON is one of Robin's OLDEST companions and appears in the earliest ballad, Robin Hood and the Monk (Child 119). He is the youngest of the original band -- 'Much' is a name meaning 'small' or 'little' (an English miller's-son standard nickname). His father the miller was murdered by the Sheriff's men; Much joins Robin for revenge. T3: WILL SCARLET is the DANDY of the Merry Men -- so called because he dresses in SCARLET SILK rather than the practical Lincoln green of the rest. In the earliest ballads (Robin Hood and the Monk, Child 119) his name is spelled SCARLOCK or SCATHELOCK -- 'Scarlet' is a later phonetic drift, encouraged by the actual red silk clothing. He is Robin's COUSIN in the later Elizabethan tradition (Anthony Munday), and often paired with Little John in dueling contests. T4: ALAN-A-DALE (or Allen-a-Dale) is a WANDERING MINSTREL who joins in the ballad Robin Hood and Allen a Dale (Child 138, printed c. 1650). His beloved is being forced by her father to marry an OLD KNIGHT for money. Alan meets Robin, tells his story, and Robin swears to help. On the wedding day Robin BURSTS INTO THE CHURCH dressed as a harper, denounces the forced marriage, and (with Friar Tuck presiding) MARRIES ALAN AND HIS BELOVED on the spot. T5: the composition of the Merry Men GROWS across the centuries -- Little John and Much and Scarlet in the earliest ballads (fifteenth century), Friar Tuck by c. 1475, Maid Marian by the sixteenth century in the May-games, Alan-a-Dale by the seventeenth-century broadsides. Every retelling adds and drops names; there is no fixed 'canonical' roster the way there is a fixed roster of the twelve peers of Charlemagne or the twelve apostles of Jesus. Further rungs: 'Scathelock' in the earliest text is thought to be an occupational nickname meaning 'lock-breaker' or 'raider' -- a job description, not a family name; Much's father the miller is one of the earliest examples of a background-tragedy for a supporting character in English folk-narrative; Alan-a-Dale's wedding-hijack is the source template for a thousand later 'stop-the-wedding' story climaxes.
source: PRIMARY: Robin Hood and the Monk (Child 119, MS c. 1450 -- Much the Miller's Son and Scathelock/Scarlet); A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117, all three as ongoing companions); Robin Hood and Allen a Dale (Child 138, broadside c. 1650). SCHOLARLY: J. C. Holt, Robin Hood (1982); Stephen Knight, Robin Hood (2003). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Merry Men', 'Will Scarlet', 'Much the Miller's Son', 'Alan-a-Dale' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia same articles -- named companions, Scarlet/Scathelock spelling drift, Alan-a-Dale's wedding rescue. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: earliest attested spelling of Scarlet/Scathelock and the exact ballad number for Alan-a-Dale.
framing_note: The MERRY-MEN roster ladder -- teach-before-test for figures who otherwise show up only as passing names. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Will Scarlet's real ballad-name is SCARLOCK or SCATHELOCK, and 'Scarlet' came later from his actual red silk clothes) and T4 (Alan-a-Dale is a MINSTREL whose beloved is being forced to marry an old knight, and Robin BURSTS INTO THE CHURCH to marry them). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Robin's minstrel companion' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a lute-carrying young man weeping under an oak, a bride at the altar with an old bridegroom, a red-silk-clad dandy dueling with a staff) and let the recall be the MERRY MAN, the OLDEST NAME, or the DEED. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the naming of Achilles's Myrmidons or the twelve peers of Charlemagne -- the hero's inner circle by name. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Merry Men (Little John, Friar Tuck, Maid Marian -- all adjacent-real from other ladders), other 'stop-the-wedding' stories (Lohengrin, Ivanhoe's Rebecca), other red-clad heroes. Wrong spelling: earliest ballad spelling is SCATHELOCK, not Scarlet.
history_overlap: None with history -- these are ballad figures. Overlaps only with each other and with the parent Robin Hood ladder.

name: The Sheriff of Nottingham: the unnamed villain of the ballads
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The Merry Men's chief enemy, and the honest note that the ballads NEVER name him. T1: the SHERIFF OF NOTTINGHAM is Robin Hood's chief enemy -- the corrupt royal official who tries to catch Robin and his men and hang them from the walls of Nottingham Castle. T2: an ENGLISH SHERIFF (from Old English 'scir-gerefa', the shire's reeve) was the KING'S TAX COLLECTOR and LOCAL LAW-ENFORCER in a shire in medieval England -- responsible for collecting fines, running the shire court, and mustering militia. It was one of the most POWERFUL and most HATED offices in the countryside, because sheriffs profited personally from every fine they levied. T3: in the earliest Robin Hood ballads the Sheriff has NO GIVEN NAME -- he is simply 'the Sheriff' or 'the high Sheriff of Nottingham'. He never gets a Christian name, a family name, or a coat of arms in the Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117), Robin Hood and the Monk (Child 119), or Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne (Child 118). His villainy is his OFFICE, not his individuality. T4: in A Gest of Robyn Hode the Sheriff proclaims a great ARCHERY CONTEST as a trap to lure Robin out of hiding. Robin comes in DISGUISE and wins the contest with the longbow. When he reveals himself, the Sheriff sends men after him and Robin escapes into Sherwood; later, in Robin Hood and the Monk, the Sheriff CAPTURES Robin while he is at prayer in a church in Nottingham, and Little John and Much the Miller's Son rescue Robin by ambushing the Sheriff's messenger and killing him with an arrow. T5: the Sheriff's DEATH in Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne (Child 118): after Robin has beheaded Guy of Gisborne and disguised himself in Guy's horse-hide cloak, Robin uses Guy's horn to summon the Sheriff, who thinks Guy has slain Robin. Robin shoots the Sheriff with his longbow before the Sheriff can escape. Further rungs: the historical Sheriffs of Nottingham of the thirteenth century -- men like Philip Marc and Brian de Lisle -- were genuinely brutal administrators of King John's regime and are the likely REAL-WORLD source of the ballad's villain; later retellings (Ivanhoe, Howard Pyle, etc.) invent names like 'Sir Guy of Gisborne as Sheriff' or 'Sir Reginald' -- these are inventions; being SHERIFF for a year in medieval England was a hazardous appointment -- most sheriffs ended their term in debt to the crown.
source: PRIMARY: A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117, the Sheriff and the archery contest); Robin Hood and the Monk (Child 119, the church capture and rescue); Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne (Child 118, the Sheriff's death). HISTORICAL: Philip Marc as historical Sheriff of Nottinghamshire under King John (c. 1209-1224); Magna Carta's clause 50 dismisses Philip Marc by name from royal service. SCHOLARLY: J. C. Holt, Robin Hood (1982) -- Sheriff as office not individual; Stephen Knight, Robin Hood (2003). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sheriff of Nottingham' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Sheriff of Nottingham', 'High Sheriff of Nottinghamshire', 'Philip Marc'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the Sheriff dies by Robin's arrow or by Little John's in Guy of Gisborne (variants exist).
framing_note: The VILLAIN ladder for the whole Robin Hood cycle. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the Sheriff has NO GIVEN NAME in any of the earliest ballads -- his villainy is his OFFICE) and T5 (Robin shoots the Sheriff with a longbow after tricking him into approaching, wearing Guy of Gisborne's horse-hide disguise). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Robin's chief enemy at Nottingham' AND ask what office he holds; describe the SCENE (a royal official at the walls of a stone castle, an archery contest as a trap, a horn call luring a rider into an arrow) and let the recall be the OFFICE, the CITY, or the WEAPON. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Prince John in Ivanhoe or Ganelon in the Song of Roland -- the corrupt royal official as story-villain. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Nottinghamshire officials (Prince John, the constable of Nottingham Castle, the Bishop of Hereford -- another ballad villain), other legendary sheriffs, other 'nameless villain' tropes. Wrong name: NO GIVEN NAME in the earliest ballads -- 'Sir Reginald' etc. are Victorian inventions.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual medieval Sheriffs of Nottinghamshire (Philip Marc named in Magna Carta 1215, Brian de Lisle) and the actual office; theology owns the ballad-VILLAIN who represents the type.

name: The archery contest at Nottingham: Robin splits the arrow (a Scott embellishment)
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The most famous Robin Hood scene, and the honest source rail. T1: the SHERIFF OF NOTTINGHAM sets a great ARCHERY CONTEST in the town square of Nottingham, with a SILVER ARROW as the prize, hoping that Robin Hood will not be able to resist trying to win it. T2: Robin comes DISGUISED (a peasant with a patch over one eye in some versions, a red-clad stranger in others). He beats every other archer at the target. T3: the SCENE in A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117) -- Robin cleaves the target from a great distance, wins the silver arrow, unmasks himself, and escapes into Sherwood with the Merry Men before the Sheriff's men can close on him. In the Gest, Robin does NOT split anyone else's arrow -- he wins by shooting nearest the mark. T4: the ARROW-SPLITTING image (Robin's second arrow SPLITTING the shaft of his opponent's arrow already in the bullseye) is NOT in the medieval ballads at all. It is SIR WALTER SCOTT'S embellishment in the novel IVANHOE (1819), chapter 13 -- where Scott has 'the yeoman' (Locksley, whom the reader gradually realises IS Robin Hood) SHOOT the arrow of his rival Hubert directly down the middle. T5: because Ivanhoe was one of the most-read novels of the nineteenth century, the arrow-splitting scene became THE iconic Robin Hood moment in every twentieth-century retelling, film, and children's book -- so much so that people assume it is medieval. Actually the trick shot is 1819 Scottish romantic novelist. The Errol Flynn 1938 film and every subsequent adaptation traces the scene through Ivanhoe, not through the ballads. Further rungs: the silver arrow as prize is authentically medieval -- silver-arrow archery contests were held in English towns down to the eighteenth century; the shot-through-the-arrow trick is physically possible with modern arrows and has been reproduced by Byron Ferguson and other trick-shot archers, though it is vanishingly rare; the arrow-splitting is so iconic that a whole class of legendary trick-shots is called 'a Robin Hood' by modern archers.
source: PRIMARY (medieval): A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117, the Sheriff's archery contest as trap, Robin winning with the disguised entry). PRIMARY (nineteenth-century embellishment): Sir Walter Scott, Ivanhoe (1819), chapter 13 -- the arrow-splitting scene. SCHOLARLY: J. C. Holt, Robin Hood (1982) -- clearly noting the arrow-splitting as Scott's invention; Stephen Knight, Robin Hood (2003). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Robin Hood in popular culture', 'Ivanhoe' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Robin Hood', 'Ivanhoe', 'Robin Hood (1938 film)'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the exact chapter of Ivanhoe and the exact wording Scott uses ('cleft the peg', etc.).
framing_note: The ICONIC-SCENE ladder with the honest source-rail. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the arrow-splitting shot is NOT in any medieval ballad -- it's Sir Walter Scott's IVANHOE 1819 embellishment) and T5 (Ivanhoe was so popular that every film since has used the scene, and everyone thinks it's medieval). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Robin's most famous shot' AND ask what it was; describe the SCENE (a silver arrow as prize, a crowd around a target, an arrow splitting another shaft down the middle) and let the recall be the WEAPON, the SOURCE-NOVEL, or the ACT. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as William Tell shooting the apple (a legendary trick-shot). DISTRACTOR MINE: other Ivanhoe scenes (the tournament of Ashby, the storming of Torquilstone Castle), other trick-shots in legend (Odysseus shooting through twelve axe-heads, William Tell shooting the apple), other 'later addition' scenes commonly assumed medieval. Wrong source: NOT in the medieval ballads -- Sir Walter Scott, Ivanhoe (1819).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Sir Walter Scott the actual Scottish novelist (1771-1832) and his career; theology owns his ADDITIONS to the Robin Hood LEGEND.

name: Guy of Gisborne: the horse-hide disguise and the beheading
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The darkest ballad in the Robin Hood cycle, from Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne (Child Ballad 118). T1: SIR GUY OF GISBORNE is a fearsome BOUNTY HUNTER who has come to Sherwood Forest to KILL ROBIN HOOD for the price on his head. He wears a strange cloak made of a WHOLE HORSE'S HIDE -- head, mane, tail and all -- to look terrifying. T2: Robin and Little John have quarrelled and separated. Robin, alone in the forest, meets the horse-hide-clad Guy of Gisborne, not knowing who he is. They FIGHT with SWORDS. Meanwhile Little John, elsewhere in the forest, is captured by the Sheriff and lashed to a tree to be hanged. T3: the FIGHT between Robin and Guy is long and vicious. Robin trips on a tree root and falls; Guy stands over him with the sword raised. Robin prays to the Virgin Mary; recovers; and stabs Guy through the heart. T4: Robin then does something SHOCKING -- he BEHEADS Guy of Gisborne, sticks the severed head on the point of his own bow, and SLASHES THE FACE with a knife until it is unrecognisable ('I'll not let his mother know him'). He then STRIPS OFF the horse-hide cloak and PUTS IT ON himself, wearing the head. T5: disguised as Guy, Robin walks up to the Sheriff (who has tied Little John to the tree) and blows Guy's HUNTING HORN as a signal. The Sheriff thinks Guy has succeeded and killed Robin. When the Sheriff comes close, Robin cuts Little John free with a knife, hands him Guy's own bow, and Little John kills the Sheriff with an arrow shot 'in his heart-blood'. Further rungs: Guy of Gisborne is likely a NAMED yeoman-outlaw of Yorkshire who existed as a real figure in the 13th century -- an outlaw turned crown-agent, whose name attaches to the ballad-villain; the horse-hide cloak is the strangest visual in the entire Robin Hood corpus -- it echoes shamanistic disguise traditions and has been proposed as a survival of a much older ritual pattern; this ballad is DARKER than the general tone of the Merry Men cycle -- Robin's mutilation of the corpse and his coldness in tricking the Sheriff are grim, and this is one reason it survived only in later manuscript form (Child 118 comes from a c. 1650 MS, but the story is clearly older).
source: PRIMARY: Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne (Child Ballad 118, MS c. 1650 but internal language suggests fifteenth-century origin). SCHOLARLY: J. C. Holt, Robin Hood (1982) -- Guy as adaptation of a real Yorkshire outlaw and the horse-hide as ritual survival; Stephen Knight, Robin Hood (2003). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Guy of Gisborne', 'Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia same articles. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the exact wording of Robin's disfigurement line ('I'll not let his mother know him' or variants); the manuscript date.
framing_note: The DARKEST Robin Hood ladder -- this is the ballad the sanitised film versions leave out. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Robin BEHEADS Guy, sticks the head on his bow-point, MUTILATES the face, then PUTS ON the horse-hide cloak himself) and T5 (Robin walks up to the Sheriff wearing Guy's skin, blows his horn as a signal, and Little John kills the Sheriff with Guy's own bow). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Robin killed a bounty hunter and wore his skin' AND ask the name; describe the SCENE (a hunter in a whole-horse-hide cloak stalking through Sherwood, a duel that ends with a head on a bow-point, an outlaw putting on the hide) and let the recall be the VICTIM, the DISGUISE, or the WEAPON used to kill the Sheriff. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Cuchulainn's warp-spasm mutilations at the Tain Bo Cuailnge or Beowulf tearing off Grendel's arm -- the DARK side of hero-legend, not softened. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Robin Hood villains (the Sheriff, the Prioress of Kirklees, the Bishop of Hereford), other beheading-and-wearing-skin motifs (Perseus with Medusa's head, in Greek pillar). Wrong hide: HORSE-hide, not stag-hide or wolf-hide.
history_overlap: HISTORY may own the possible historical Yorkshire outlaw named Guy of Gisborne; theology owns the ballad-VILLAIN and the horse-hide episode.

name: Robin's death at Kirklees: bled by the prioress, one last arrow
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The end of the Robin Hood cycle, from A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117, final fitte) and Robin Hood's Death (Child Ballad 120). T1: at the end of his outlaw career ROBIN HOOD falls ILL and goes to KIRKLEES PRIORY (a Cistercian nunnery in Yorkshire) to be BLED. Bleeding -- draining a measured amount of blood from a vein -- was the standard medieval remedy for fevers. T2: the PRIORESS OF KIRKLEES, Robin's OWN COUSIN in the Gest, is his enemy secretly. She agrees to bleed him and takes him to a chamber in the priory. T3: the Prioress opens the vein in Robin's arm and then LEAVES HIM ALONE, locking the door -- so that his blood DRAINS OUT slowly and he WEAKENS to death. The bleeding-to-death is deliberate murder disguised as a botched medical procedure. T4: LITTLE JOHN, waiting outside, hears Robin's WEAKENING HORN-CALL and forces his way into the chamber. Little John begs to burn Kirklees Priory to the ground in revenge, but Robin FORBIDS it -- 'I never hurt a woman in all my life, nor man in woman's company'. T5: Robin, dying, asks Little John to bring him his BOW and one final ARROW. He shoots the arrow OUT OF THE OPEN WINDOW and asks Little John to bury him WHEREVER THE ARROW FALLS. Little John finds the arrow and buries Robin in Kirklees Park with the bow beside him. Further rungs: an old grave in KIRKLEES PARK in West Yorkshire has been shown as Robin's grave since at least the seventeenth century -- the stone slab has been chipped away by souvenir hunters over generations; the involvement of the Prioress and Sir Roger of Doncaster (her paramour in some versions) as conspirators appears in the Gest but is compressed in Child 120; the story of shooting an arrow to mark one's grave is echoed in the Norse burial of Sigurd and in the archery-death traditions of English yeoman-hero songs; the whole ending is the DIGNIFIED HERO'S DEATH, not a battle-death -- Robin dies of BETRAYAL by a woman of his own family, and forgives even her.
source: PRIMARY: A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child Ballad 117, final fitte -- Robin at Kirklees, the Prioress's betrayal, the arrow-marks-the-grave); Robin Hood's Death (Child Ballad 120, broadside c. 1650 -- a more compressed version of the same ending). SCHOLARLY: J. C. Holt, Robin Hood (1982) -- the Kirklees location and the traditional grave; Stephen Knight, Robin Hood (2003). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Death of Robin Hood', 'Kirklees Priory' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'A Gest of Robyn Hode', 'Kirklees Priory', 'Robin Hood's Grave'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the Prioress is named or unnamed in the Gest, and Sir Roger of Doncaster's role.
framing_note: The DEATH-OF-A-LEGEND ladder -- the mandatory closer for the Robin Hood arc. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Robin is BLED to DEATH by his own COUSIN the Prioress) and T5 (he shoots one last ARROW OUT THE WINDOW to mark his own GRAVE). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Robin was killed by the Prioress of Kirklees' AND ask how she killed him; describe the SCENE (an old outlaw at a nunnery, a bleeding-vein remedy that goes wrong on purpose, a weakening horn-call, an arrow through an open window) and let the recall be the VILLAINESS, the METHOD, or the FINAL SHOT. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the death of Roland at Roncesvalles, the death of Cuchulainn tied to the stone, or the death of Baldr by mistletoe -- the great hero's END is a moment of dignified betrayal, not a battle-defeat. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Robin Hood women (Maid Marian is not involved; the Bishop of Hereford is a different villain), other medieval hero-deaths (Arthur at Camlann, Roland at Roncesvalles), other 'bury me where X' burial-instructions (King Arthur's Avalon, Charlemagne's Aachen). Wrong location: KIRKLEES PRIORY, not Sherwood Forest itself.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Kirklees Priory as an actual Cistercian nunnery dissolved by Henry VIII in 1539; GEOGRAPHY owns the Yorkshire location. Theology owns the LEGEND-death that happened at that priory in ballad.

name: Roland at Roncesvalles: the rearguard betrayed by Ganelon
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The great chanson de geste of medieval France, the Song of Roland (c. 1100, Oxford Digby 23 manuscript). T1: ROLAND is a knight of CHARLEMAGNE, King of the Franks and Holy Roman Emperor; Roland is Charlemagne's NEPHEW and one of the TWELVE PEERS of France, the emperor's closest paladins. T2: as Charlemagne's army returns from a long campaign in SPAIN across the mountains of the PYRENEES, Roland is given command of the REARGUARD -- the last twelve peers of the army guarding the rest as they cross a narrow mountain pass called RONCESVALLES. T3: unknown to Charlemagne, a Frankish traitor named GANELON has SOLD OUT the rearguard's position and timing to the Saracen king Marsile. As Roland's rearguard passes through Roncesvalles, a Saracen army of a hundred thousand ambushes them from the surrounding cliffs. Roland's men are outnumbered a hundred to one. T4: Roland's best friend, OLIVER, begs Roland to blow his HORN OLIFANT ('elephant', made of a great ivory tusk) to call Charlemagne back before it's too late. Roland REFUSES three times -- he says it would be dishonourable to summon help before he has personally faced the enemy. Only after most of the rearguard is dead, and Roland himself is bleeding, does he agree. When he finally blows Olifant, he blows it with such force that the VEINS in his TEMPLES BURST -- but Charlemagne, thirty leagues away, HEARS the horn and turns his army back. It is too late; the rearguard is doomed. T5: Roland fights on with his sword DURANDAL (see next ladder) and dies on the hillside, laying himself down FACING SPAIN so that Charlemagne will see he died attacking, not retreating. The Archbishop TURPIN, a fighting bishop of Charlemagne's court, dies beside Roland after slaying dozens of Saracens; the two die on the same field. Further rungs: the historical event under the legend is the ambush of Charlemagne's rearguard at Roncesvalles Pass in AUGUST 778 by BASQUES (not Saracens) -- the chanson three centuries later has recast the Basques as Muslim Saracens to serve the crusading mood of the late eleventh century; the Song of Roland was chanted by a jongleur called TAILLEFER before the Battle of Hastings in 1066 to inspire the Norman troops (recorded by Wace); the manuscript we have is Oxford Digby 23, copied c. 1140-1170, containing 4,002 lines of Old French decasyllables in laisses (rhymed stanzas).
source: PRIMARY: La Chanson de Roland (Song of Roland), Oxford Digby 23 MS (c. 1140-1170; text composed c. 1100). Notably laisses 83-127 (Roland refuses the horn), 129-135 (Roland finally blows Olifant, the temple-vein bursts), 168-176 (Roland's death facing Spain). HISTORICAL: Einhard, Vita Karoli Magni chapter 9 (c. 830 -- the actual ambush at Roncesvalles Pass in August 778 by Basques); Annales regni Francorum for the year 778. LATER TESTIMONY: Wace, Roman de Rou (c. 1160) on Taillefer chanting the Song at Hastings 1066. SCHOLARLY: Joseph Bedier, La Chanson de Roland (1922 edition); Gerard Brault, The Song of Roland: An Analytical Edition (1978). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Song of Roland', 'Roland (paladin)' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'The Song of Roland', 'Battle of Roncevaux Pass'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact laisse numbers for the horn-blowing scene and the temple-vein rupture.
framing_note: The FOUNDATIONAL Roland ladder -- teach-before-test anchor for Durandal, Olifant, Ganelon, Turpin, and the whole chanson cycle. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Roland refuses to blow the horn until it's TOO LATE, and when he does the VEINS IN HIS TEMPLES BURST from the force) and T5 (Roland lies down FACING SPAIN so his king will see he died attacking). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Charlemagne's nephew at the pass' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a narrow mountain pass, a rearguard of twelve knights against a hundred thousand, a horn blast from a bursting temple-vein) and let the recall be the KNIGHT, the PASS, or the HORN. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Norse Ragnarok, the Greek Achilles's final rampage, or the Christian martyrdom of Stephen -- a doomed stand rendered as sacred story. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Charlemagne peers (Oliver, Turpin, Ganelon the traitor -- all adjacent-real from the same chanson), other last-stands (Leonidas at Thermopylae, Cuchulainn tied to the stone), other betrayal-figures. Wrong enemy: the chanson names them Saracens; the historical enemy at Roncesvalles was BASQUES -- honest legend-vs-history distinction.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual 778 ambush at Roncesvalles Pass by Basques (Einhard's Vita Karoli, Annales regni Francorum) and Charlemagne's Spanish campaigns; theology owns the CHANSON version composed three centuries later where the enemy is Saracens and the traitor is Ganelon.

name: Durandal: the unbreakable sword and the split rock
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: Roland's sword in the Song of Roland (c. 1100, Oxford Digby 23). T1: DURANDAL is the SWORD of the paladin ROLAND, nephew of Charlemagne; it is described in the Song of Roland as the greatest and sharpest sword in Charlemagne's army. T2: the relics in Durandal's hilt: the chanson (laisse 173) says Roland's sword-hilt contains a TOOTH OF SAINT PETER, BLOOD OF SAINT BASIL, HAIR OF SAINT DENIS (the Frankish national saint), and a PIECE OF THE ROBE OF THE VIRGIN MARY -- turning the sword into a portable reliquary as well as a weapon. T3: as Roland lies dying at Roncesvalles, he realises that his sword must not be captured by the pagans and turned against Christian knights. He tries to DESTROY DURANDAL by SMASHING IT AGAINST A GREAT ROCK. T4: the STONE SPLITS but DURANDAL DOES NOT BREAK -- Roland strikes the rock with all his fading strength again and again, and the rock cracks and shatters, and the sword rings and remains WHOLE. Roland gives up trying to break it, hides it beneath his body, and dies. T5: a NOTCHED CLEFT in a cliff wall at ROCAMADOUR in southern France has been shown as 'Roland's cleft' (la Breche de Roland) since the middle ages -- pilgrims are told this is the split Roland made trying to break Durandal; a sword called Durandal was displayed at the Rocamadour sanctuary as a relic from the twelfth century onwards. Further rungs: the name 'Durandal' means 'enduring' or 'the one that lasts', from Latin durare (to endure); other legends give the sword to Hector of Troy first, thence via a series of owners to Roland (a way of tying French chivalric myth back to the Trojan founding-legends of European kingship); Charlemagne's own sword in the chanson is JOYEUSE ('joyful'), separately named; the Rocamadour Durandal was reportedly STOLEN in June 2024 -- an actual news event that generated headlines about the legend.
source: PRIMARY: La Chanson de Roland (Song of Roland), Oxford Digby 23 MS, laisses 171-173 (Roland's attempts to break Durandal, the relics in the hilt); laisses 174-175 (Roland lies down with Durandal under him and dies). LATER LEGEND: the twelfth-century Cistercian sanctuary at Rocamadour and the sword displayed there. SCHOLARLY: Joseph Bedier, La Chanson de Roland (1922); Gerard Brault, The Song of Roland: An Analytical Edition (1978). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Durandal', 'Rocamadour' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Durendal', 'Rocamadour', 'Chanson de Roland'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the exact laisse numbering for the relics-list and the rock-breaking scene; the June 2024 news about the Rocamadour theft.
framing_note: The NAMED-WEAPON ladder for the Roland cycle. Dinner-test payoff: T3+T4 (Roland tries to BREAK his own sword against a great ROCK to keep it from the enemy -- the ROCK SPLITS, the SWORD does NOT) and T2 (the sword-hilt held a TOOTH of Saint Peter, BLOOD of Saint Basil, and hair from Saint Denis). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Roland's sword' AND ask what it was called; describe the SCENE (a dying paladin striking a great rock with his blade, a cliff cracking open, a sword staying whole in his hand) and let the recall be the SWORD, the ROCK, or the RELICS. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Excalibur returned to the lake, Mjolnir at the wager, or Gae Bolg thrown by Cuchulainn -- a named hero-weapon with its own drama. DISTRACTOR MINE: other named chivalric swords (Excalibur of Arthur, Joyeuse of Charlemagne himself, Tizona of El Cid, Curtana the sword of mercy of English coronations, Notung of Sigurd -- all adjacent-real), other unbreakable-sword tales, other holy-relic weapons. Wrong owner: DURANDAL belongs to ROLAND, not to Charlemagne (whose sword is Joyeuse).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual sanctuary at Rocamadour and the June 2024 theft of the Durandal relic-sword; GEOGRAPHY owns Rocamadour as a real place. Theology owns the LEGEND of the sword that split the rock.

name: Charlemagne's revenge: hanging Ganelon and mourning at Aachen
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The closing act of the Song of Roland (c. 1100, Oxford Digby 23), CHARLEMAGNE'S grief and vengeance. T1: after CHARLEMAGNE hears Roland's dying horn-blast and turns his army back, he arrives at RONCESVALLES too late to save the rearguard -- Roland, Oliver, Archbishop Turpin, and the entire twelve peers are dead on the mountainside. T2: Charlemagne, weeping so hard that his BEARD is soaked, orders his army to pursue and destroy the Saracen force that killed Roland. He pursues them all the way to the RIVER EBRO in Spain, where the pagans drown in the swollen river as the Christians press them from behind. T3: Charlemagne then gathers his army and marches home to AACHEN (Aix-la-Chapelle), his capital, to bury Roland with honour. But before the burial the traitor GANELON, who sold out the rearguard to the Saracens, must face judgement. T4: Ganelon is tried before Charlemagne and the assembled peers. Ganelon's kinsman PINABEL fights a JUDICIAL DUEL on his behalf against Roland's kinsman THIERRY. Thierry, though the smaller man, WINS the duel; God grants him victory as a sign of Ganelon's guilt. T5: Ganelon is executed by being TORN APART BY FOUR HORSES -- each of his four limbs tied to a wild horse, the horses driven off in four directions until his body is quartered (laisse 289). Thirty of Ganelon's kinsmen are hanged. Charlemagne, at the last, is visited in a dream by the angel GABRIEL who tells him he must ride out to yet another war -- the aged emperor weeps and cries 'God, how weary is my life!' (Dieu, si penuse est ma vie!) -- and the chanson ends on that note of exhaustion, not triumph. Further rungs: the four-horse dismemberment is one of the medieval extreme punishments reserved for high treason -- also used in France for the assassin Ravaillac in 1610; the historical Charlemagne is buried in AACHEN CATHEDRAL, whose octagonal Palatine Chapel he built around 800; the Song of Roland's final line 'Ci falt la geste que Turoldus declinet' names TURoldus as the poet or reciter -- one of the very few named authors of a chanson de geste.
source: PRIMARY: La Chanson de Roland (Song of Roland), Oxford Digby 23 MS, laisses 176-291 (Charlemagne's pursuit to the Ebro, Roland's burial, Ganelon's trial, Pinabel-Thierry duel, Ganelon's dismemberment, Charlemagne's dream). HISTORICAL: Einhard, Vita Karoli Magni chapters 27-33 (Charlemagne's palace at Aachen and his burial there in 814). SCHOLARLY: Joseph Bedier, La Chanson de Roland (1922); Gerard Brault, The Song of Roland: An Analytical Edition (1978). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Ganelon', 'Song of Roland', 'Aachen Cathedral' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Ganelon', 'The Song of Roland', 'Charlemagne'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: laisse numbering for Ganelon's execution and the final line naming Turoldus.
framing_note: The AFTERMATH ladder for the Song of Roland -- the revenge, the trial, the exhaustion. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (Ganelon is torn apart by four horses tied to his limbs; Charlemagne is visited by the angel Gabriel telling him to ride out yet again, and the chanson ENDS on 'God, how weary is my life') and T4 (Ganelon's guilt is proved by JUDICIAL DUEL). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the traitor of the Song of Roland' AND ask who he was; describe the SCENE (a Frankish emperor weeping into his beard, a betrayer's kinsman fighting for him in single combat, four wild horses tied to a man's limbs) and let the recall be the TRAITOR, the PUNISHMENT, or the LAST LINE. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Odysseus's slaughter of the suitors, David's mourning for Absalom, or the Norse Sigurd cycle's vengeance patterns -- vengeance that is both righteous and exhausting. DISTRACTOR MINE: other chanson figures (Oliver, Turpin, Roland himself), other trial-by-combat stories (Ivanhoe's rescue of Rebecca), other medieval traitors (Judas Iscariot from a different pillar, Mordred from Arthurian). Wrong death: TORN APART BY FOUR HORSES, not hanged or beheaded.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual Charlemagne (742-814), his capital at Aachen, his Palatine Chapel, and his burial there; theology owns the CHANSON version of his grief and his vengeance on Ganelon.

name: El Cid: Rodrigo Diaz, exile of Alfonso VI, and the swords Tizona and Colada
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The great Castilian epic Cantar de Mio Cid (c. 1207) and its hero. T1: RODRIGO DIAZ DE VIVAR was an eleventh-century Castilian knight who became one of the greatest warriors of his age. His nickname EL CID comes from the Arabic AL-SAYYID meaning 'the lord' -- Muslim opponents and Christian allies alike gave him the honorific. T2: the Cantar de Mio Cid (Poem of My Cid, c. 1207 manuscript, oldest surviving Castilian epic) opens with Rodrigo being UNJUSTLY EXILED from Castile by King ALFONSO VI of Leon and Castile after enemies at court whisper against him. Weeping, Rodrigo leaves his wife DONA JIMENA and daughters at the monastery of San Pedro de Cardena and rides out with a small band of followers into exile. T3: the exiled Cid supports himself and his men as a MERCENARY CAPTAIN, campaigning across Christian and Muslim al-Andalus. He wins the first cantar of the poem with plunder from Alcocer and gifts them to Alfonso VI as tribute, hoping to earn back the king's favour. T4: Rodrigo wields TWO NAMED SWORDS in the Cantar: COLADA (won in battle from the Count of Barcelona) and TIZONA (won from the Moroccan king Bucar). Both swords are so famous that later cantar-audiences would gasp at their names alone. In the third cantar of the poem the Cid gives Colada and Tizona to his sons-in-law -- and then TAKES THEM BACK after the sons-in-law dishonour his daughters. T5: after years of exile the Cid conquers the great city of VALENCIA (see next ladder) and eventually reconciles with Alfonso VI. The Cantar's third cantar centres not on more battles but on the LAWSUIT the Cid brings against his sons-in-law for their cowardice and cruelty; the Cid wins the case in Alfonso's court, and the daughters are re-married to the princes of Navarre and Aragon -- the marriage from which, the poem says, all the Christian kings of Spain descend. Further rungs: the historical Cid died in Valencia in 1099; his sword TIZONA is actually preserved -- an eleventh-century sword traditionally identified as the Cid's is on display at the Museum of Burgos, though its authenticity is disputed by historians; the historical Cid served both Christian and Muslim kings during his career -- he was for a time in the pay of the Muslim emirs of Zaragoza -- the epic tidies this into a purely Christian arc; the name 'Campeador' (battler) is a second nickname for him.
source: PRIMARY: Cantar de Mio Cid (Poem of the Cid), unique MS Vitr. 7-17 in the Biblioteca Nacional de Espana; text composed c. 1140-1207 (manuscript colophon 1207 by Per Abbat). Notably lines 1-13 (the exile begins), lines 3060-3200 (the Cortes at Toledo and the lawsuit), lines 3730-3740 (Colada and Tizona named). SCHOLARLY: Ramon Menendez Pidal, La Espana del Cid (1929); Colin Smith, The Making of the Poem of the Cid (1983). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'El Cid', 'Cantar de Mio Cid' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'El Cid', 'Cantar de mio Cid', 'Tizona', 'Colada'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the disputed authenticity of the Museum of Burgos Tizona and the exact line-numbers for the swords' introduction.
framing_note: The FOUNDATIONAL El Cid ladder -- teach-before-test anchor for the Valencia and the death-on-horseback ladders. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (EL CID means 'THE LORD' in ARABIC, and it was his MUSLIM opponents who gave him the title) and T4 (his two swords have names -- COLADA and TIZONA -- and he took them back from his sons-in-law after they beat his daughters). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the great Castilian knight' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (an exiled warrior riding out from Burgos, a man who fought for both crescent and cross, a swordsman with two named blades) and let the recall be the KNIGHT, the CITY he conquered, or the SWORDS. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Roland at Roncesvalles or Cuchulainn at the ford -- the culminating warrior of a national epic. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Christian-Muslim frontier figures (Bernardo del Carpio the legendary Spanish knight, James I of Aragon), other named swords (Durandal of Roland, Excalibur of Arthur, Joyeuse of Charlemagne, Tyrfing of the Volsungs), other epic exiles. Wrong king: ALFONSO VI of Leon and Castile, not Alfonso VII or Sancho.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar (c. 1043-1099), his historical career serving both Christian and Muslim rulers, and his conquest of Valencia in 1094; theology owns the CANTAR version and the two named swords as story-objects. GEOGRAPHY owns Valencia and Burgos as real places.

name: The Cid conquers Valencia: siege, feast, and the wife brought to the tower
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The middle cantar of the Cantar de Mio Cid, the great victory of the Cid's career. T1: after years of exile campaigning in the frontier lands of eastern Iberia, the CID and his growing band of Christian warriors lay SIEGE to the great Muslim city of VALENCIA on the Mediterranean coast. T2: the SIEGE lasts NINE MONTHS. The city is starved and finally surrenders. The Cid enters Valencia in 1094 (in the historical event) and takes the city with all its riches, though he treats the Muslim inhabitants (in the poem's telling) with unusual generosity for the age. T3: the Cid's WIFE DONA JIMENA and his two DAUGHTERS Elvira and Sol have remained at the monastery of SAN PEDRO DE CARDENA throughout the exile. Now, with Valencia won, the Cid sends for them. When Jimena and the daughters arrive at Valencia, the Cid takes them up to the TOP OF THE ALCAZAR (the great fortress-palace) to show them 'their new home' -- the city they can see stretching out in every direction. T4: the news of Valencia's fall spreads across al-Andalus. The Almoravid king Yusuf of Morocco crosses the strait and lands a huge army to try to retake Valencia. The Cid rides out and DEFEATS Yusuf's army on the plain outside the city, capturing so much treasure that his men are enriched for life. He sends 200 horses to KING ALFONSO VI as tribute, and this is the beginning of his reconciliation with the king who exiled him. T5: the Cid gives his daughters ELVIRA and SOL in marriage to the INFANTES DE CARRION (princes of a great Leonese house), a match arranged by Alfonso VI himself. The wedding feast at Valencia is one of the great scenes of the second cantar -- but the marriage will end in disaster (see next ladder). Further rungs: the historical siege of Valencia lasted from 1092 to 1094 and the Cid ruled Valencia as an independent lord until his death in 1099; his widow Jimena held Valencia for THREE MORE YEARS after his death, only surrendering to the Almoravids in 1102 when the situation became impossible; the Alcazar of Valencia was destroyed centuries later, but the site is now the Plaza de la Almoina.
source: PRIMARY: Cantar de Mio Cid (Poem of the Cid), MS Vitr. 7-17 Biblioteca Nacional de Espana, cantar 2 lines 1610-2277 (siege of Valencia, arrival of Jimena and daughters, defeat of Yusuf, wedding of the daughters to the Infantes de Carrion). HISTORICAL: contemporary Latin chronicle Historia Roderici (c. 1110) and Muslim historian Ibn Alqama's now-lost account. SCHOLARLY: Menendez Pidal, La Espana del Cid (1929); Colin Smith, The Making of the Poem of the Cid (1983). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Siege of Valencia', 'Cantar de Mio Cid' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Siege of Valencia (1092-1094)', 'Cantar de mio Cid'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: dates and length of the siege; Jimena's tenure after Rodrigo's death.
framing_note: The MIDDLE-CANTAR VICTORY ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Cid brings his wife and daughters up to the top of the ALCAZAR to show them the CITY he has won as their new home) and T4 (the Almoravid Yusuf lands an army from Morocco to retake Valencia, and the Cid rides out and defeats it). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the Cid captured the great Mediterranean city' AND ask which one; describe the SCENE (a nine-month siege, a starved city surrendering, a warrior taking his family up to a fortress tower to show them their new home) and let the recall be the CITY, the WIFE, or the ENEMY KING. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Odysseus's return to Ithaca reunited with Penelope, or David bringing the Ark up to Jerusalem -- a warrior installing his family in the seat of his victory. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Reconquista sieges (Toledo 1085, Zaragoza 1118, Seville 1248 by Ferdinand III), other Muslim invasions of Iberia (Tariq ibn Ziyad at Gibraltar 711), other Almoravid figures. Wrong city: VALENCIA, not Toledo, not Seville, not Zaragoza.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual Reconquista siege of Valencia (1092-1094), the Cid's rule of Valencia as an independent lord, and the Almoravid campaigns; theology owns the CANTAR version. GEOGRAPHY owns Valencia as a real Mediterranean port city.

name: The Cid dead on horseback: strapped to Babieca to rout the Almoravids
strand: Western myth: Robin Hood + Roland + El Cid + medieval legends
scope: The most famous post-Cantar legend of the Cid, not from the Cantar de Mio Cid itself but from later medieval Castilian chronicles. T1: in 1099 the CID dies of illness in his Valencian palace, worn out by decades of war. T2: even as the Cid lies dying, the Almoravid army under king Bucar has laid siege to Valencia hoping to retake it. If the news of the Cid's death gets out, the defenders' morale will collapse and Valencia will fall. T3: the legend told in the Estoria de Espana (late thirteenth century) and repeated in later chronicles: DONA JIMENA and the Cid's followers KEEP HIS DEATH SECRET. They EMBALM his body, put on his armour, and STRAP his corpse UPRIGHT to his warhorse BABIECA. T4: at dawn the Valencia garrison opens the gates and the Cid's corpse -- lance and shield in place, upright in the saddle -- LEADS the CHARGE out against the Almoravid camp. The Almoravids, seeing the Cid still alive and coming for them, panic and rout; thousands drown trying to flee across the Mediterranean. T5: after the victory the Cid's body is taken back across Spain to the monastery of SAN PEDRO DE CARDENA (where his wife had waited during his exile years) and there entombed with all honour. The horse Babieca is buried at the same monastery in a special grave, according to legend, and after Babieca is gone Jimena refuses to let anyone else ride any horse of that stable. Further rungs: this dead-on-horseback story is NOT in the Cantar de Mio Cid itself -- the Cantar ends with the Cid alive at his daughters' remarriage. The legend appears in the Alfonso X chronicle Estoria de Espana in the late thirteenth century and is the invention of that chronicle-tradition; historically Valencia DID hold out for about three years after the Cid's death and was surrendered by Jimena in 1102 to the Almoravids -- the last-battle-on-horseback is legend layered over history; the horse Babieca in the Cantar is one of the Cid's most-praised possessions; his tomb is today at Burgos Cathedral, moved from San Pedro de Cardena in the nineteenth century.
source: PRIMARY (legend): Estoria de Espana (late 13th century, commissioned by Alfonso X of Castile); the Cronica de Veinte Reyes (early 14th century) repeats and elaborates the dead-on-horseback story. NEGATIVE PRIMARY: Cantar de Mio Cid ends before the Cid's death; the dead-charge is a LATER legend. HISTORICAL: Rodrigo dies at Valencia in July 1099; historically Valencia was surrendered by Jimena in 1102 without the dead-Cid battle. SCHOLARLY: Menendez Pidal, La Espana del Cid (1929) -- the layering of legend over history; Colin Smith, The Making of the Poem of the Cid (1983). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'El Cid', 'Babieca' (via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'El Cid', 'Estoria de Espana', 'Babieca', 'Battle of Valencia (1099)'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact source-attribution for the dead-charge (Alfonso X's Estoria vs Cronica de Veinte Reyes vs the later Corneille play Le Cid 1636).
framing_note: The MOST FAMOUS Cid legend ladder, with the honest source-rail (this is chronicle-legend, not from the Cantar). Dinner-test payoff: T3+T4 (the Cid's corpse is STRAPPED UPRIGHT to his horse BABIECA and LEADS THE CHARGE out of Valencia -- the Almoravids see him coming and PANIC). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the Cid rode out dead' AND ask on what horse; describe the SCENE (a warrior's embalmed corpse in full armour, an upright figure in a saddle riding at the head of a sortie, an enemy army fleeing before a dead man) and let the recall be the HORSE, the ENEMY, or the RELIC. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Achilles's ghost rallying the Achaeans, or the Norse tradition of the einherjar fighting on after death, or Sigurd's ride through fire -- the DEAD-HERO trope, unsoftened. DISTRACTOR MINE: other famous warhorses (Bucephalus of Alexander the Great, Marengo of Napoleon, Traveller of Robert E. Lee, Sleipnir of Odin), other dead-hero legends, other Reconquista battles. Wrong horse: BABIECA, not Al-Borak (the Prophet's steed) nor other named mounts.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual death of Rodrigo Diaz in Valencia in 1099 and the actual 1102 surrender of Valencia to the Almoravids; theology owns the LEGEND of the dead-charge, layered by Alfonso X's chronicles in the late thirteenth century.
